name: Kuot
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Lindström, Eva. 2002. Topics in the grammar of Kuot, a non-Austronesian language of New Ireland, Papua New Guinea. PhD dissertation, Department of Linguistics, Stockholm University. ISBN 91-7265-459-7.
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 Phonology, §3.5 'Stress', p. 112; section summary and ex. (88) p. 117; chapter overview p. 85 (author-posted chapter PDF of the dissertation, native).
catalog_quote: Kuot stress is lexically determined, i.e., there are no general stress rules that make reference to syllables or moras, but the position of stress has to be known for each lexeme. Some endings frequently attract stress in combination with lexical stems, but particular stems retain stress even when such an ending is present. Preliminary analysis yields the following generalization: Lexical stress in Kuot is manifested chiefly through duration, but is not associated with pitch. Rather, pitch appears to be used mainly to signal information about the clause. ... The first word in Figure 2 is the noun ŋa'ne 'meat or vegetable to go with tubers or rice', and the second is the adjective 'ŋane 'strong-3m'. ... The words are ka'ranim 'reef, low tide; year' and 'baranim 'store; net for catching birds'. ... In summary, pitch is used primarily for intonation (the topic of the next section), while word stress is achieved primarily through duration. [p. 85 overview:] Stress is not predictable from general principles (i.e., it is lexical), and is manifested primarily as duration. It is distinct from pitch which functions separately to signal intonational information
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kuot is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Lindström & Remijsen 2005 (Linguistics 43(4): 839-870), is squarely about Kuot word stress and intonation; only its abstract could be read (OpenAlex), which states that word stress is lexically determined, duration-cued, with no F0 correlate. The full text is closed access with no repository copy, and every open route tried by automated download (De Gruyter/degruyterbrill landing and PDF: HTTP 202 empty; Edinburgh Research Explorer: an automated-access block/404; Remijsen's archived homepage: citation only, no PDF; DiVA: connection refused; scholar.archive. BASE: bot-gated; the Internet Archive's index: offline; The best first-hand stress statement actually read is Lindström's 2002 thesis, section 3.5 Stress (pp. 112-117; the chapter PDF and text were already held by the project from an earlier reading and were read in full): stress is lexical, must be known per lexeme, realised chiefly as duration and not pitch, with minimal pairs and occasional grammatical stress shift. New records saved: OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar metadata JSONs and the 2020 Internet Archive copy of Remijsen's Edinburgh publication list, all logged in Since there is no catalog record, supersedes_catalog_source is false; the thesis section would be the deciding source for a new Kuot entry (lexical stress), with the 2005 paper as the stronger phonetic confirmation once obtained.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (44 pp., Distiller 2002, native text; extracted text, no scanned). PDF page 28 carries the printed folio 112 and the heading '3.5 Stress'; the quoted passage is there word for word (only differences are the footnote callouts 13/14/15 that the quote drops): 'Kuot stress is lexically determined, i.e., there are no general stress rules that make reference to syllables or moras, but the position of stress has to be known for each lexeme. Some endings frequently attract stress in combination with lexical stems, but particular stems retain stress even when such an ending is present. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress position is a lexical property of each lexeme; there is no syllable- or mora-based rule. It is cued by duration (with some intensity), not by pitch, which is used for clause intonation. Minimal pairs: ŋa'ne 'meat/vegetable accompaniment' vs 'ŋane 'strong-3m'; ka'ranim 'reef, low tide; year' vs 'baranim 'store; bird net'. Chapter opening (p. 85): 'Stress is not predictable from general principles (i.e., it is lexical), and is manifested primarily as duration.' Summary (p. 117): 'pitch is used primarily for intonation.. while word stress is achieved primarily through duration.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Author notes a possible 'combination of two stressed syllables' in a word when a stem with inherent stress carries a stress-attracting enclitic (duk 'thunder' + subject enclitic), but treats interactions as beyond scope (p. 117).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift is occasionally an exponent of a grammatical category: future of some class II verbs, e.g. i-abǝ ['jabǝ] 'she climbs' vs i-aba [ja'ba] 'she will climb' (ex. 88, p. 117). Some grammatical morphemes often but not always attract stress, notably the non-singular suffix -(i)p on nouns and the subject enclitics of verb class I. Possible inherent stress distinguishing homophone pairs duk 'break/thunder', ut 'be full/be like'. Footnote 13 (p. 112): stress is not marked on Kuot forms in the thesis because the author distrusted her early transcriptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word (lexeme) level stress within the grammatical word; demonstrated on words in utterance-final, sentence-medial and topicalised-phrase positions with instrumental figures (Figs 2-5b, pp. 113-116); pitch belongs to clause-level intonation (§3.6). Analysis explicitly labelled 'preliminary'.
new_statements.identity_note: Lindström's description is based on fieldwork in Bimun village (west coast, southern Kuot area); she notes that Panaras (northern) speakers regard their dialect as more original and that the SIL Chungs worked at Kabil on the east coast. No dialect glottocodes under kuot1243 were seen; the statement is taken as language-level for kuot1243.

The catalog_records entry for Kuot (src world-r2-2026-09-17) has an empty rule field; this source fills it with 'lexical/unpredictable, duration-cued, no fixed-position coding'. The listed open_url (the Harvard library catalogue) served only a JavaScript shell with no full-text link; the DiVA record it points to (diva2:19184) timed out; the chapter PDFs already held by the project (from the author's Stockholm thesis page via the the Internet Archive, see) were read instead.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical and unpredictable: no syllable- or mora-based rule; the stress position must be listed for each lexeme. Minimal pairs are given (ŋa'ne 'meat/vegetable side dish' vs 'ŋane 'strong-3m'; ka'ranim 'reef, low tide; year' vs 'baranim 'store; bird net', pp. 113-116). Stress is realised chiefly by duration (with some intensity), not by pitch, which carries clause intonation (§3.6). The chapter overview (p. 85) restates it: 'Stress is not predictable from general principles (i.e., it is lexical), and is manifested primarily as duration.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated. The author raises the possibility that a stem with inherent stress plus a stress-attracting subject enclitic yields 'the combination of two stressed syllables' (duk 'thunder', p. 117) but says such interactions are complex and beyond the study's scope.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Stress shift marks the future in some class II verbs: i-abǝ ['jabǝ] 'she climbs' vs i-aba [ja'ba] 'she will climb' (ex. 88, p. 117). (b) Some grammatical morphemes 'often, but not always, attract stress', notably the non-singular suffix -(i)p on nouns and the class I subject enclitics (p. 117). (c) Fn. 13, p. 112: stress was hard for the author to perceive, so stress is not marked on cited forms in the thesis; the analysis is called preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Lindström 2002 describes Kuot of New Ireland (title); the stress section carries no dialect qualification. Instrumental pairs were recorded from two male speakers in their thirties (p. 113).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Chung & Chung 1996 (index 0, reported not-opened): now opened via the the Internet Archive copy of the SIL PDF and read in full after scanned. It contains no statement on word stress; the one prosodic remark is p. 10 (polar questions vs declaratives differ 'only in intonation': clause-final rising vs descending pitch). Appendix A (pp. 73-75) transcribes forms with stress marks at varying positions ('luguan-tuan, pa'pa-ruan, kumo'rot-tuan, olabu'an-tuo, aga'bunima-ruo, nap-'up..), which is implicit support for lexically variable placement but not a rule statement. Nothing else was missed; only two works were listed and both are now checked.

sources.quote: Word stress, on the other hand, does not interact with intonation in terms of its encoding. It displays a very stable correlation with duration but no association with F 0 ; in other words, there is no consistent marking of stress by means of F 0 in Kuot. The position of Kuot word stress is lexically determined, yielding minimal stress pairs. [...] A phonetic analysis of minimal stress pairs recorded in controlled environments demonstrates that lexically stressed syllables do not correlate with pitch.
